title: Start with what you already have
summary: Don't buy a rack on day one. Use the old laptop or a $20–60 Marketplace OptiPlex.

start.body:
You don't need to spend money to start a home lab.

A home lab is just a computer you leave on — so you can try things without breaking the laptop you write email on.

The first lab is usually an old laptop that still turns on, or a retired office PC someone is giving away.

what-counts.body:
What counts as "enough"?

• Turns on and shows a screen
• Has about 8 GB of memory (RAM) or more — that's the short-term sticky notes inside the computer
• Has a real ethernet (network cable) port if you can find one — Wi‑Fi works too

You do not need a rack, a NAS, or a new mini PC yet.

look.body:
Look in the closet, guest room, drawer of chargers, or the shelf behind the TV.

A five-year-old laptop is fine. A small office box (Dell OptiPlex, HP EliteDesk, Lenovo ThinkCentre) is fine.

What do you already have?

choices.label: I already have a box that boots

have-box.body:
Leave it plugged in. That is the lab.

Learn on it first. A quieter or newer mini PC waits until this one is actually in the way — after you've used it for real.

dedicate-check.body:
Is this computer still someone's daily machine (school, work, the only family laptop)?

If yes: don't wipe it yet. Borrow time on it later, or find a second box.

If it's spare: you can dedicate it — meaning this computer's main job becomes "the lab."

choices.label: It's spare — I can dedicate it

daily-caution.body:
Keep the OS it has for now. Don't erase a machine people still need.

You can still continue — next you'll pick an OS for a future dedicated box, or wait until you find a spare.

dedicated-ok.body:
Good. A dedicated box can be wiped and given a simple Linux later.

Before you erase anything: copy off photos or papers you care about. Empty machine? You're already done.

marketplace.body:
Marketplace, Buy Nothing, or a friend clearing a desk.

Ask for: boots to a desktop or login screen, about 8 GB+ memory, and a real ethernet port if possible.

Skip giant loud 1U rack servers for now — they suck power and sound like a leaf blower.

marketplace-budget.body:
Budget: $0–60 is plenty for a first box.

Names you'll see: OptiPlex, EliteDesk, ThinkCentre, NUC. "Tiny" / "micro" / "mini" usually means it sits quiet on a shelf.

If the seller says "no hard drive," that's OK — a used SSD is cheap later. Confirm it powers on.

loud.body:
Use the loud one for a week anyway.

You'll learn whether you actually leave a computer on overnight. If the noise still bothers you after that, look at a quiet tiny PC — only then.

power-note.body:
Power-hungry boxes also cost more on the electric bill if you leave them on 24/7.

For a first lab, a laptop or tiny office PC is usually quieter and cheaper to run than a big tower with a gaming GPU.

marketplace-wipe.body:
If it came from Marketplace: wipe before you trust it.

"Wipe" means erase the disk and install a fresh OS so old accounts and mystery software are gone.

Already wiped and dedicated? You'll pick an OS in the next walkthrough.

skip-buys.body:
Skip buying on day one:

• A rack or rack rails
• A new managed switch
• A NAS "starter kit"
• Used 1U space heaters
• 10‑gig networking

You are allowed to spend later. You are not required to spend to start.

stuck-find.body:
If you're stuck finding hardware:

• Ask one friend who works in an office — retired PCs get tossed often
• Check local Buy Nothing with "desktop" or "laptop"
• A used Chromebook is a weak lab (locked-down); prefer a regular Windows/Linux-capable PC

Still nothing? Pause this project. Come back when a box appears — the next steps wait.

ready.body:
You're set for the idea of a first lab: one spare computer, left on, nothing fancy bought yet.

Next comes picking an OS — what the computer boots into. Resume from your ByteRush feed when you are ready.

end.body:
You have reached the end of this walkthrough.

Remember: the lab is the habit of leaving something on and learning — not the shopping cart.

why-lab.body:
Why leave a computer on?

So services can sit there: a file share, photo backups, a small website for the house.

Your daily laptop can sleep. The lab stays awake.

ram-check.body:
How to check memory (RAM) quickly:

• Windows: Settings → System → About — look for "Installed RAM"
• Mac: Apple menu → About This Mac
• If it won't boot far enough: anything that ran Windows 10 with 8 GB is usually fine

4 GB can work for learning; 8 GB is more comfortable.

ethernet-gloss.body:
Ethernet = the plastic network cable click-port (looks like a fat phone jack).

Wi‑Fi works. Cable is steadier for a box that lives in a closet.

You do not need a new switch yet — one cable into your existing router or Wi‑Fi is enough.

habit.body:
The real milestone isn't hardware.

It's the habit: one machine you treat as "always on," where it's OK to experiment.

Breakages stay on the lab, not on the family laptop.

not-yet.body:
Things that can wait months:

• Fancy UPS (battery backup)
• Homelab Reddit shopping lists
• Matching rackmount everything

Learn the boring path first.
